results.content: # Struct with specific byte size and layout. I'm attempting to follow along with this series discussing how to build a simple sqlite clone and I'm attempting to write it in Rust. I'm having trouble understanding how to achieve the serialization that is done in C, in Rust. So (in C) there is a struct to represent a Row. And the layout of the struct once serialized is very exact -. image723×170 5.38 KB. Attempting to recreate that same struct in rust however gives very different results. The size of the struct ends up being 1152 bytes instead of the expected 291, what is the reason for the difference and how could I achieve the layout that I need here? println!("Row occupies {} bytes.", size_of::<Row>());. The reason for the difference is that Rust's `char` and C's `char` are not the same at all: in Rust `char` is a Unicode scalar value and is 4 bytes, while in C it is just one byte. ~~However, note that in Rust structs layout is not guaranteed: you need to add `#[repr(C)]` to make it "like C".~~ I see you already have it, sorry. Although `packed` is not the default in C. Also, I would recommend to not rely on structs for serializations but rather use proper serialization/deserialization (probably with serde) because padding can sneak and serialization is hard in general. results.title: Endianness, API Design, and Polymorphism in Rust
results.content: I have been working on a serialization project recently that involves endianness (also known as byte order), and it caused me to explore parts of the Rust standard library that deals with endianness, and share my thoughts about how endianness should be represented in a programming language and its standard library, as I think this is also something that Rust does better than C++, and also makes for a good case study to talk about API design and polymorphism in Rust. Indeed, if we want to display a byte as a series of bits, we as the programmer get to choose the endianness, and the program runs identically on either a big endian or a little endian platform. We want to write a number – say, `2000` – in big endian, but we don’t want to think of it as bytes, yet. So we byte swap the number, and instead of storing `2000`, we store `3490119680`, so that if we write it using the processor’s normal mechanism for writing, it comes out to 2000 in big endian. struct Structure { a: u32, b: u32, c: u32, } impl Structure { fn serialize(&self, endianness: Endian) -> [u8; 12] { let mut res = [0u8; 12]; [0..4].copy_from_slice(self.a.to_endian_bytes(endianness)); [4..8].copy_from_slice(self.b.to_endian_bytes(endianness)); [8..12].copy_from_slice(self.c.to_endian_bytes(endianness)); res } pub fn serialize_old_version(&self) -> [u8; 12] { self.serialize(Endian::Big) } pub fn serialize_new_version(&self) -> [u8; 12] { self.serialize(Endian::Little) } }. For example, if there were a platform where 4-byte chunks were split into 2-byte chunks little endian, but 2-byte chunks were split into 1-byte chunks big endian, we could write a new policy for this platform and all the existing code would support it. This means that if we were writing in C++, we would have enough from this informal protocol to write a function that did something like “write this value in big endian twice, and little endian twice, to different locations” that was agnostic to the type provided, as long as it implemented this informal interface. What if we want to make decisions about endianness at run-time, say, because we are implementing DBus?

results.content: # A Beginner’s Guide to Go Struct Layout and Padding (And Why It Matters). The truth is, understanding struct layout and padding can make a big difference in how efficient and clean your code is. In this guide, I’ll break it down in plain English: what struct layout is, why padding exists, and how you (yes, even as a beginner!) can start writing smarter, more optimized Go structs. type Example struct { A byte // 1 byte B int32 // needs 4-byte alignment}. type Example struct { A byte // 1 byte B int32 // 4 bytes C byte // 1 byte}. A [1] + pad [3] → B [4] → C [1] + pad [3] = 12 bytes total. Half the struct’s size is actually padding! * **Memory usage**: Poorly arranged structs can waste a lot of space, especially if you’re working with big arrays or slices. // Less optimaltype Bad struct { A byte B int64}. // Bettertype Good struct { B int64 A byte}. A [1] + pad [7] → B [8] → total: 16 bytes. B [8] → A [1] + pad [7] → total: 16 bytes. While the total size here stays the same, when you pack **many** of these structs into a slice or array, the difference can add up if the compiler can collapse padding across elements. type Example struct { A byte B int64}. * `A` → 1 byte Padding → 7 bytes (to align `B`). * `B` → 8 bytes = Total **16 bytes** per struct. If you store **one** struct, it’s 16 bytes. But if you store **100 structs in a row**, Go **might** optimize the space between them (because the end of one struct’s last field aligns perfectly with the start of the next), effectively reusing the padding instead of doubling it. To help you order your struct fields efficiently, here’s a quick reference of common Go types sorted by their typical size (on a 64-bit machine):. Struct layout and padding might feel like low-level details you can ignore — and most of the time, Go handles them for you.

results.title: What is padding in Python? - Quora
results.content: What is padding in Python? In Computer science, padding is usually a term that describes the act of taking a value, and adding pad characters to the left or right (or both) sides of a string in order to fix the length of the string; either for output formatting, processing or encryption (some encryption processes are stable and more secure wen the strings are a fixed length). Padding in Python refers to adding extra characters (most commonly spaces, zeros, or other fill characters) around or inside a string or numeric representation so it meets a specified width, alignment, or format. Padding in Python refers to adding extra characters (most commonly spaces, zeros, or other fill characters) around or inside a string or numeric representation so it meets a specified width, alignment, or format. + struct.pack("4s x 2s") uses explicit pad bytes in format strings (x = pad byte). Padding in Python is the deliberate insertion of characters (space, zero, custom fill, or null bytes) to reach a required width or alignment, implemented via string methods (ljust/rjust/center/zfill), format specifications (f-strings, format()), and binary tools (struct, manual byte padding). Padding in Python is implemented by ljust, rjust, and center function on a string.Few usecases are to give margins to String, Password encryption and user required string manipulation. results.title: Endianness: Byte Reversal Explained - Little vs Big Endian
results.content: Essentially, endianness defines the order in which bytes of a multi-byte data type are stored in computer memory. In little-endian systems, the least significant byte (LSB) is stored first, followed by the other bytes in descending order of significance. Consider a 32-bit integer: its representation in memory will differ significantly between little-endian and big-endian systems.
